title: Asking for directions
script: Student: Excuse me, is the campus library open on Sundays?
context: Student asks about Sunday library hours.

questions.question: Which response is most appropriate?
options: Yes, it opens at ten in the morning.
The librarian wrote a history book.
My dorm is behind the hospital.
questions.explanation: A direct response answers the question about Sunday opening hours.

title: Rescheduling a meeting
script: Student: Could we move our project meeting to Thursday afternoon?
context: Student asks to change the day of a project meeting.

questions.question: Choose a natural reply.
options: The project is made of wood.
questions.explanation: The natural reply confirms availability for the proposed time.

title: Printing at the library
script: Student: I need to print my assignment, but my account balance is zero. Staff: You can add credit at the kiosk near the entrance. Student: Is the kiosk available after six? Staff: Yes, but the main help desk closes at six.

questions.question: What problem does the student have?
questions.explanation: The student explicitly says the printing account balance is zero.

questions.question: What remains available after six?
questions.explanation: The staff says the kiosk remains available after the desk closes.

title: Research poster deadline
script: Student: I thought our poster was due Friday. Adviser: The deadline moved to Wednesday because printing takes two days. Student: Should we submit the final PDF through the course site? Adviser: Yes, and keep a copy for the department archive.
context: A student discusses a revised deadline.

questions.question: Why did the deadline change?
questions.explanation: The adviser links the earlier deadline to printing time.

questions.question: What should the student submit?
options: A final PDF on the course site
Only a link to the archive
questions.explanation: The adviser confirms submitting a final PDF on the course site.

title: Safety drill notice
script: Attention all students: The science building will hold a scheduled fire drill on Tuesday at 2 p.m. Please leave using the nearest marked exit and meet staff in the east courtyard. Do not use elevators during the drill. Classes will resume after the all-clear announcement.

questions.question: Where should students meet?
questions.explanation: The announcement specifies the east courtyard.

questions.question: What should students avoid?
questions.explanation: The instruction says not to use elevators.

title: Art exhibition opening
script: Good afternoon. The student art exhibition opens at four on Friday in the central gallery. Visitors may enter free of charge. A short artist talk begins at five, and the gallery will close at seven. Photography is allowed, but please do not use flash.

questions.question: When does the artist talk begin?
questions.explanation: The announcement says the artist talk starts at five, one hour after the exhibition opens.

questions.question: What is the photography rule?
questions.explanation: Photography is allowed but flash is prohibited.

title: How Pollinators Support Crops
script: Many flowering plants rely on insects to move pollen between flowers. Bees are familiar pollinators, but butterflies, beetles, and flies also play important roles. Habitat loss can reduce the variety of pollinators in an area. Farmers sometimes plant strips of native flowers near fields to provide food and shelter. However, the impact of such strips depends on the surrounding landscape and the seasons when plants bloom. Researchers therefore measure pollinator visits over time rather than counting flowers only once.

questions.question: What is the central topic?
options: The contribution of different insects to pollination
questions.explanation: The speaker explains pollinators and habitat strategies.

questions.question: Why measure visits across time?
options: To account for changes across seasons and conditions
questions.explanation: Visits vary, so repeated observations help assess effects.

title: The Limits of Historical Maps
script: A historical map tells us something about how people understood a place at the time it was drawn. Yet maps can omit areas their makers knew little about, and boundaries may reflect political claims rather than verified measurements. Historians compare maps with travel notes, census records, and archaeological evidence to identify these limitations. A discrepancy does not always mean the mapmaker made a mistake; sometimes different sources used different names or purposes.

questions.question: Why might boundaries on a map be unreliable?
options: All old maps were made from photographs
questions.explanation: Some boundaries represent claims rather than verified measurements.

questions.question: How do historians check the map?
options: By assuming one map is perfect
questions.explanation: The speaker recommends comparing travel notes, census records, and archaeological evidence.
